note: THE COMPOUNDING ASSET. Every fact we verify gets stored here with how we know it. Instruments can be copied in a weekend; a decade of verified, sourced, dated knowledge cannot. This file is the thing that is actually worth something in five years.
law: A fact enters only with: the claim, at least one named source, the date verified, who verified it, and what would prove it wrong. No entry may be added from memory. An entry with no falsifier is an opinion and belongs in house-theses.md instead.

confidence.VERIFIED: multiple independent sources, or one primary source (official Pokémon/TPCi, a grader's own published data, or our own measurement)
confidence.SINGLE-SOURCE: one credible source, no corroboration found — publishable with attribution and a hedge
confidence.COMMUNITY: repeated across independent community voices but not documented anywhere primary — publishable only as community lore, explicitly labelled
confidence.DISPUTED: credible sources disagree — publish the disagreement, never a resolution we invented
confidence.REASONED: an argument from principle rather than a sourced fact - defensible, not verified, and labelled so nobody treats it as settled
confidence.UNKNOWN: we have looked and do not know. Recorded so the gap is visible rather than filled in with a plausible number.

facts.claim: The English Wizards Black Star Promo Moltres, Articuno and Zapdos credit Toshinao Aoki. The connecting painting is by Naoyo Kimura. Collectors call the first print the Aoki error. They were given away the second week of The Power of One, 21 July 2000, not 1999.
sources: Wikipedia: Pokémon the Movie 2000 (US theatrical 21 July 2000)
facts.falsifier: a first-print English Wizards promo 21–23 that credits Kimura on the card, or a primary Wizards source dating the giveaway to 1999

facts.claim: Shadowless is not a rarity tier or a stamp. It is the earliest English Base Set printing, before Wizards of the Coast added a drop shadow to the right and bottom of the artwork window.
facts.falsifier: a primary Wizards of the Coast source showing the shadow change was a deliberate edition rather than a mid-run design change

facts.claim: Base Set is the only main English expansion with no set symbol beside the artwork.
sources: Big Orbit Cards: Base Set identification guide
facts.falsifier: any other main English expansion printed without a set symbol

facts.claim: The commonly repeated figure of 10,000 copies per 1st Edition Base Set card has never been confirmed by Wizards of the Coast or The Pokémon Company.
sources: Fanatics Collect auction description stating the figure has never been confirmed
facts.falsifier: a primary source publishing an actual print-run figure
facts.note: Published as an unconfirmed-claim story, never as a print-run number. This entry exists partly to stop US repeating it.

facts.claim: Shining Fates booster packs were never sold separately at retail; they came only inside special collections.
facts.falsifier: evidence of a retail single-pack SKU for Shining Fates
facts.note: Drives the break-out pack rule: loose Shining Fates packs are genuine but were opened out of collections, which prices differently.

facts.claim: eBay's final value fee on trading cards is 13.25% plus a per-order fee, calculated on item plus shipping plus tax.
facts.falsifier: a fee schedule change; this is a moving number and must be rechecked
facts.note: Downgraded by our own knowledge guard on first run: one source is not VERIFIED, even when the source is the company setting the fee. Corroborate with a second reference or an actual invoice before promoting.

facts.claim: TCGplayer market price is an item price and does not include shipping; sellers set shipping separately by product size.
sources: TCGplayer help: How is shipping applied to marketplace orders
TCGplayer help: What Should I Charge for Shipping
facts.falsifier: TCGplayer publishing a shipping-inclusive market figure
facts.note: This is why our eBay-vs-TCG comparison is not like-for-like, and why we label rather than estimate the difference.

facts.claim: The set identifier swsh45 refers to Shining Fates, not SWSH Promos.
facts.falsifier: an official source mapping swsh45 to a different set

facts.claim: No external body publishes a sealed Pokémon index, so our index level cannot be independently corroborated — it is internally consistent rather than externally verified.
sources: absence of any published sealed index at time of writing
facts.falsifier: any third party publishing a comparable sealed index we could check against
facts.note: Recorded so we never let VERIFIED on the index be read as externally corroborated.

facts.claim: Recurring content topics in the Pokemon TCG creator space include: TCG prices, tracking the market, hidden gems, plays nobody is talking about, and reprints.
facts.falsifier: search or platform data showing these topics are not among the recurring themes creators cover
facts.note: Recorded as founder knowledge rather than measured demand. If we ever get real search data, promote or correct it — but it is the best source we have and better than guessing.

facts.claim: On X, shorter posts generally outperform longer ones for reach, and posts containing external links typically see reduced distribution.
facts.falsifier: our own posting data showing longer posts or link posts performing equally

facts.claim: Loose booster packs and sleeved booster packs are both single packs, from different origins. A LOOSE pack comes from opening a sealed product — a box, ETB or bundle. A SLEEVED pack comes from a case, or is bought singly from a store.
facts.falsifier: evidence that sleeved and loose packs are the same product or that either is not a single pack
facts.note: CONSEQUENCE FOR OUR FILTER: excluding the term "sleeved" removes an entire legitimate class of single pack. It killed 318 listings across the board. Origin also plausibly affects price — a loose pack came out of a box somebody had access to, a sleeved pack did not — so they may deserve separate tracking rather than a merged median.

facts.claim: Single pack pricing should come from TCGplayer rather than eBay, because packs are a commodity class where TCGplayer is the deeper and more representative venue.
facts.falsifier: mapped TCGplayer pack prices persistently sitting above eBay asks for the same SKU
facts.note: ALREADY IMPLEMENTED for price. NOT implemented for LISTING COUNT, which still comes from eBay — so a pack row currently shows a TCGplayer price beside an eBay listing count, which are two different markets in one line.

facts.claim: English ABRA and KADABRA cards both stopped after Expedition Base Set in September 2002 and did not return until 2023 - a twenty-one year gap for BOTH. Alakazam partially escaped, appearing in 2009, 2019 and 2020. Uri Geller sued over Kadabra's Japanese name Yungeraa, objecting to Dark Kadabra portraying it as evil; The Pokemon Company stopped producing the line. Geller gave his blessing in 2023.
sources: our own card catalogue - every English Kadabra print, 1999 to 2025
our own catalogue: every English print year for Abra, Kadabra and Alakazam
facts.falsifier: an English Kadabra card printed between September 2002 and September 2023
facts.note: CORRECTED ON VERIFICATION. Several sources state the gap ran from 1997, but our own catalogue holds English Kadabra cards from Base 1999, Base Set 2 2000 and Expedition 2002. The lawsuit-era gap is 2002 to 2023, twenty-one years - still the longest absence of a Pokemon from the TCG, and still an extraordinary story. Publishing the 26-year figure would have been repeating a number three secondary sources agree on and our own primary data disproves. FOUND BY THE THEME SCOUT, 2026-08-23: I recorded this as a Kadabra story. The agent searched every print year in the catalogue and showed the gap covers ABRA TOO - the pre-evolution, which is not named in any article about the lawsuit. And that ALAKAZAM kept being printed in 2009, 2019 and 2020, so the ban was not line-wide. That is a better and more precise story than the one I wrote, and I would not have found it by remembering harder. Tyler's point exactly: the agents see what I do not.

facts.claim: Koga’s Ninja Trick had its artwork changed before international release because it featured a manji, a Buddhist symbol used on Japanese temples and maps, which resembles a swastika. The two symbols are distinct - opposite orientation, dots in the corners, not rotated - but every print including later Japanese reprints used the updated artwork.
facts.falsifier: a post-change print carrying the original manji artwork
facts.note: Publish the distinction carefully: the manji is a Buddhist symbol, not a Nazi one, and saying so accurately is the whole point of covering it.

facts.claim: Misty’s Tears had its Japanese artwork replaced for international release. Rather than editing the original, The Pokemon Company commissioned an entirely new illustration from Ken Sugimori showing Misty crying while Squirtle tries to catch her tears.
facts.falsifier: evidence the replacement art was edited from the original rather than newly commissioned
facts.note: The interesting part is not the censorship, it is that they paid Sugimori to draw a whole new card rather than crop one.

facts.claim: The first Pokemon card banned for being too powerful was Super Energy Removal from the original Expansion Pack, banned in 1999 and initially only in Japanese tournaments. Over 62 cards have been banned in some capacity since.
facts.falsifier: an earlier power-based ban, or a materially different total

facts.claim: No cards are currently banned in the Pokemon TCG Standard format. Archeops and others are banned in Expanded.
sources: pokemon.com official Pokemon TCG Banned Card List
facts.falsifier: the official list adding a Standard-format ban
facts.note: A primary source. Worth citing whenever the topic comes up, because most articles about bans are about Expanded or about censorship and conflate the three.

facts.claim: Posting a cropped card ILLUSTRATION without the card frame is a weaker nominative fair use position than posting the whole card, because nominative use rests on identifying a product and a bare crop presents the artwork as artwork.
sources: US trademark nominative fair use doctrine
our own ARTIST CLAIM LAW and IP-depiction register entry
facts.falsifier: counsel advising that a cropped illustration carries the same protection as a full card image
facts.note: Not a reason to avoid it - the format performs five times better and the whole hobby posts card art. It is a reason to CAPTION it: name the card, the set and the illustrator on every art crop, which restores the identifying purpose and credits the person who drew it. That is cheap, correct, and better content anyway.

facts.claim: Serving card artwork from our own domain is a materially different act from linking to the rights-holder’s host. Hotlinking embeds an image the owner is already serving; hosting a copy means we are the one distributing it.
sources: US copyright practice on reproduction and distribution
our own compliance register, pokemon-ip-depiction entry
facts.falsifier: counsel advising the two carry equivalent exposure
facts.note: This does NOT mean do not do it - the whole hobby hosts card images and it is the only way to make downloads work reliably. It means the IP consult moves up the queue: it was triggered by the first dollar, and hosting artwork is a second trigger that arrives sooner. Mitigations that cost nothing: credit the illustrator on every image, state we are unaffiliated with Nintendo/TPCi, and remove anything on request without argument. TYLER’S POSITION (Aug 23): "we aren’t doing anything wrong, just making homebrewed content from public content which is fully legal." He is right about the practical reality - fan content is everywhere and the hobby runs on it. The one distinction worth keeping straight is that publicly VIEWABLE is not the same as public DOMAIN: card art is copyrighted and fan use is tolerated rather than licensed. That distinction costs nothing while we are free and unmonetised, and it is exactly what the IP consult is for. Recording it here so the position is written down rather than argued about later.

facts.claim: Missing illustrator credits in the community card dataset are a BACKFILL LAG, not a Pokemon decision. 1-4% of cards are missing artist data for every year from 2002 to 2023, but 43.7% of 2024 cards, 29.3% of 2025 and 23.8% of 2026. Every physical Pokemon card prints "Illus. <name>" on its face, so the credit exists and the dataset has not caught up.
sources: our own card catalogue, 16,468 cards analysed by release year
facts.falsifier: a recent card with no illustrator printed on the physical card, or a statement from the dataset maintainers that the omission is deliberate
facts.note: THE OPPORTUNITY: the gap is concentrated in exactly the sets people are opening right now - Surging Sparks 252, Mega Evolution 188, Prismatic 180, Stellar Crown 175. If we backfill illustrator credits for recent sets we would hold better artist data than the source everyone else uses, and artist-based content is the lane we have already proved works. It is also the kind of contribution worth giving back upstream.

facts.claim: PSA publishes centering tolerances: Gem Mint 10 requires approximately 55/45 or better on the front and 75/25 on the reverse; Mint 9 approximately 60/40 front and 90/10 back; NM-MT 8 approximately 65/35 front. BOTH axes must pass independently - a card perfectly centred left-to-right but 60/40 top-to-bottom does not make PSA 10.
facts.falsifier: PSA publishing different tolerances, which they have done before
facts.note: SOURCES DISAGREE on whether the front-10 threshold is 55/45 or 60/40, and at least one says PSA tightened it from 60/40 to 55/45 in early 2025. The primary source says 55/45. Any tool we build must cite the primary and show the ratio, never only a verdict - because the threshold itself has moved.

facts.claim: Centering is the single most common reason an otherwise flawless card drops from a 10 to a 9.
facts.falsifier: grader-published data showing corners or surface cause more downgrades
facts.note: This is what makes centering worth measuring even though it is only one of four criteria - it is both the most measurable AND the most frequently decisive.

facts.claim: Centering can be measured from a photograph by geometry: detect the outer card edge, detect the inner artwork frame, compute the four margins and express opposite pairs as ratios. Corners, edges and surface cannot be assessed reliably from a single phone photo - surface scratches and holo scuffs are visible only at particular light angles, and corner wear needs resolution and lighting a phone rarely provides unaided.
sources: PSA grading standards on the four criteria
facts.falsifier: a demonstrated phone-only tool whose corner and surface calls match PSA outcomes at scale
facts.note: THE LINE THIS DRAWS: centering is arithmetic and auditable - every measurement traces to a detected edge. A predicted GRADE is a black box that costs somebody a submission fee when it is wrong. We can defend the first and cannot defend the second.

facts.claim: PPT supplies eBay sold-by-grade aggregates (count, median, min, max per PSA grade) on every enriched card. The block carries lastEbayCheck but NO date range for the sales themselves, so we cannot state what period a median covers.
sources: data/singles-enrichment.json - the ebaySold block on 12 cards
facts.falsifier: a PPT parameter or field that returns or states the window
facts.note: TESTABLE HYPOTHESIS, not yet proven: eBay sold listings expire around 90 days, so if PPT scrapes eBay the aggregate may ALREADY be a rolling ~90-day window that is simply unlabelled. Sample sizes lean that way - 559 PSA 10 sales over 90 days is 6.2 a day for a single card, which is high; over the 19 months since release it is 1.5 a day, which is very plausible for a chase. That reads as ALL-TIME rather than rolling, which would make the median a historical average and the withdrawal correct. But it is a reasoned read from six cards, not proof. THE DEFINITIVE TESTS, both cheap: (1) check whether PPT documents the window or accepts a period parameter, (2) snapshot the same card twice a week apart - an all-time count can only grow, so a count that DROPS proves a rolling window.

facts.claim: PPT's ebaySold graded aggregates (psa8/9/10 count, median, min, max) carry NO time window and no parameter controls one. The days parameter drives priceHistory only. Therefore a graded median from this source is a historical average of unknown period, not a current price. A separate field, smartMarketPrice, DOES carry a window (daysUsed) and a confidence, and is the only defensible graded figure available.
sources: PRIMARY — the provider's own API: a 400 from /api/v2/cards listing allowedParameters, with period, from, to and window all rejected (checked 2026-08-23)
PRIMARY — our own measurement: across days=7/90/180 metadata.historyWindow changed while the graded aggregate stayed byte-identical (White Kyurem EX, tcgPlayerId 90589, psa10 n=40, median $168.50)
PRIMARY — our own catalogue: dateRangeStart/End spans across 309 graded cards in data/enrichment-raw.ndjson vary 0-513 days, earliest 2025-03-15
facts.falsifier: A drop in any psa9/psa10 count on a later run of scripts/graded-window-probe.mjs would prove a rolling window and reverse this. Baseline 2026-08-23; recheck after 2026-08-30.

facts.claim: Attack names and flavour text are available free from the same source we already ingest - 82% of cards carry an attack name and 40% carry flavour text in a three-set sample. Our catalogue captures neither.
facts.falsifier: the source dropping those fields, or a sample showing far lower coverage
facts.note: FOUND BY A REAL POST. Tyler posted Slakoth at 2am after 17 hours of coding. Slakoth's attack is literally called TAKE IT EASY. The card wrote the joke and nothing we generate could have found it, because we hold name, artist, set, rarity, date and price - and not one word the card actually says. This is the single biggest content gap we have: the copy is already printed on the cards.

facts.claim: Rendering a realistic replica of a named grader's slab carries two distinct risks: the label design, logo and colour scheme are that company's trade dress, and a convincing fake slab image is usable to misrepresent a raw card as graded.
sources: our own compliance register, pokemon-ip-depiction entry
facts.falsifier: counsel advising that a clearly-labelled replica for visualisation carries neither exposure
facts.note: THE SECOND RISK IS THE SERIOUS ONE and it is not about us being sued - somebody lists a raw card using our PSA-lookalike render and a buyer pays graded money. That is a fraud our tool enabled. Building a CATCH'EM slab instead removes both at once, and is the better product anyway: a replica markets the grader, ours markets us, and it is the thing we would sell later. Four colourways shipped 2026-08-23.

facts.claim: The slab-protector market is established and competitive. GradedGuard sells TPU+PC cases in colourways with hobby-store exclusives and storage boxes for 12 and 36 slabs. Slabmags sells aluminium-alloy cases with UV-resistant tempered glass across PSA, BGS, SGC, TAG and CGC. Phantom Display sells the cast-acrylic Magneto at $55-60 as of July 2026. Amazon carries VALUN, X PRO, SlabX, RCPLAGA and Livresse in 4-12 packs, and Etsy carries 3D-printed custom bumpers.
facts.falsifier: these brands exiting, or a price survey showing materially different points
facts.note: THE GAP: every one of them sells colourways you CHOOSE. Not one sells rarity, blind packs, or a pull. Tyler's structure is genuinely unoccupied in a category that is otherwise well served — and GradedGuard already runs hobby-store EXCLUSIVES, which proves scarcity works here before we test it ourselves.

facts.claim: Three material tiers are in market: TPU with a polycarbonate front (GradedGuard, most Amazon brands), aluminium alloy with tempered glass (Slabmags, premium), and cast acrylic (Phantom, display-focused). 3D printing serves the low-volume custom end on Etsy.
facts.falsifier: a major entrant using a different material class
facts.note: 3D PRINTING IS THE OPENING. Etsy sellers already run it profitably at low volume, which means a first run needs no injection-mould tooling and no minimum order — the two things that normally make a physical product impossible for a solo founder. Tooling comes later, once demand is proven.

facts.claim: A simple single-cavity injection mould in China runs roughly $1,500-$5,000 in 2026. A real quoted example: a square PP box lid, 150x150x15mm, 718H steel, single cavity, quoted at $1,250. A single-cavity TPU phone-case mould starts around $3,500. Small toy parts on single-cavity aluminium run $2,000-$5,000.
facts.falsifier: quotes from three factories on OUR geometry landing outside this band
facts.note: The phone case is the closest comparable: thin shell, snap fit, TPU or TPU+PC, cosmetic finish. A slab guard is geometrically simpler - fewer undercuts, no port cutouts - so the low end of the band is plausible and the high end is safe to plan against.

facts.claim: Per-unit injection cost excluding tooling: roughly $1.50-$4.00 at 1,000 units and $0.80-$2.00 at 5,000 units for ABS-class parts. One published curve gives about $4 at 100 pieces, $2.60 at 5,000 and $1.70 at 100,000. Another gives $1.50 all-in at 2,000 units of which $1.00 is tooling amortisation.
sources: haizol.com China Injection Molding Industry Report 2026
facts.falsifier: real quotes on our part landing outside the band
facts.note: TOOLING IS THE BARRIER, NOT THE PLASTIC. At 1,000 units a $3,000 mould adds $3.00 per unit; at 5,000 it adds $0.60. The whole economic question is order size, not material.

facts.claim: Chinese factories routinely quote below the MOQs commonly assumed. One states a standard MOQ of 1,000 with small batches of 100-500 available, another advertises 500-unit pilot runs. Across 190 multi-quote RFQs, 35.5% fell below 100 units and attracted 3-7 competing factory quotes within 24 hours.
sources: haizol.com China Injection Molding Industry Report 2026
facts.falsifier: our own RFQ being refused below 1,000 units by three factories
facts.note: This is the finding that changes the plan. The received wisdom that Chinese factories will not touch small runs is contradicted by the quote data - the real constraint is that tooling is fixed, so small runs are EXPENSIVE rather than refused. 3D printing was never necessary; it was a workaround for a barrier that is not there.

facts.claim: Across 190 multi-quote RFQs the most expensive quartile was 2.0x the cheapest at the median and 2.9x in higher-spread jobs; the cheapest quartile sat 30.8% below the median, widening to 46.3% in the top quartile of spreads.
sources: haizol.com China Injection Molding Industry Report 2026
facts.falsifier: a later report showing convergence
facts.note: SINGLE SOURCE, held anyway because the ACTION it implies is free: get three quotes rather than one. Even if the exact spread is wrong, nobody has ever been harmed by comparing three quotes on an identical spec. NEVER TAKE ONE QUOTE. A single quote on this part could be double what the same job costs elsewhere, and the spread usually reflects different ASSUMPTIONS about cavity count, steel grade, finish and trial shots rather than different quality. Three quotes minimum, on an identical written spec.

facts.claim: OBS captures specific SOURCES, not the whole screen, so a separate browser window is invisible to a stream by default. OBS also supports Custom Browser Docks (Docks > Custom Browser Docks) which are private panels visible only to the presenter, and Browser Sources inside a scene which ARE visible to the audience. Both take a plain URL.
sources: obsproject.com forum thread on second outputs
facts.falsifier: OBS removing custom browser docks, or a version where docks appear in captures
facts.note: THIS IS THE WHOLE ARCHITECTURE, handed over for free: two URLs from one session. The presenter pastes one into a Custom Browser Dock and the other into a Browser Source, and OBS does the rest. No plugin, no install, no integration to maintain. It also means the private/public split is enforced by OBS rather than by us, which is far safer than us trying to hide things.

facts.claim: Every teleprompter tool surveyed scrolls text the creator has already written. Teleprompter.com, PromptSmart, FlowPrompter, Speakflow, StreamYard's built-in, Online Prompter, Transparent Teleprompter and the Elgato Prompter all take an existing script as input. None supplies subject matter.
facts.falsifier: a prompter that generates or supplies topic material rather than displaying supplied text
facts.note: THE GAP, and it is larger than it first looked. Tyler's idea is not a teleprompter — it is a CONTENT FEED for live, and the entire category is solving the opposite problem. Their users arrive with a script and need help reading it; a card creator going live has plenty to say and needs something to say it ABOUT. Nobody is building that, and we hold 16,468 cards, 33 sourced facts and 287 catalogue findings.

facts.claim: Progressive disclosure is for rare controls, never necessary ones. Hiding a core action behind 'more options' is friction dressed as minimalism, and if users cannot find a hidden feature it was not disclosed progressively — it was hidden. For small option sets (3-5) disclosure adds a click without reducing load. ChatGPT converts 95%+ of first visits on one input with no gates.
facts.falsifier: usage data showing a gated flow converting better than an ungated one
facts.note: IT NAMED EXACTLY WHAT I BUILT. The editor asked four questions before returning anything, and clicking an angle before a count returned SILENTLY because fCount started at 0. Tyler said the angle section was 'not even working' and he was right — a hidden prerequisite that fails without explanation is the worst possible failure, because the feature looks broken and says nothing. Fixed by defaulting the count and grouping the 35 themes rather than hiding them: at that size the answer is structure, not a more-options click.

facts.claim: Pikachu was not the planned face of the franchise. Satoshi Tajiri told TIME: when they made the anime they wanted a specific character to focus on, and Pikachu was chosen because it was relatively popular compared with the others and potentially both boys and girls would like it. Clefairy was Red's first Pokemon in the Pocket Monsters manga and is widely reported as the intended mascot; Poliwhirl, Tajiri's own favourite, appeared on the first Pokemon Center logo and on the cover of TIME.
sources: TIME interview with Satoshi Tajiri (primary, quoted widely)
facts.falsifier: an official statement that Pikachu was the intended mascot from the start
facts.note: THE NUANCE THAT MATTERS: Tajiri's quote confirms Pikachu was not pre-planned, and is the strongest source. The specific claim that CLEFAIRY was the planned mascot is widely repeated but its documentary trail is thinner — a 2024 Bulbagarden thread notes no official source states it outright, and infers it from the manga. Say Pikachu was not the plan; be softer on naming who was.

facts.claim: The chubby Gen 1 Pikachu design was progressively SLIMMED over subsequent generations, not preserved because of fan affection. Pikachu became the mascot through its casting in the 1997 anime, decided by the animation team for gender-neutral appeal, after Tajiri noted it was already relatively popular in the games.
facts.falsifier: a designer statement that the chubby form was retained in response to fan demand
facts.note: THIS IS THE CORRECTION. The causal chain runs: popular in the games -> cast in the anime -> mascot. It does NOT run: fans loved the chubby design -> the company improvised. And the design history points the opposite way, because the chubby form was deliberately reduced over time. 'Chunkachu' is real fan slang for the Gen 1 shape, but it is a nickname applied later, not a thing the company reacted to.

facts.claim: A Pokemon's TCG card type frequently differs from its video-game type. Lugia is Psychic/Flying in the games and Colorless on the card; Scizor is Bug/Steel and Metal; Dragonite is Dragon/Flying and Colorless. The TCG collapses the game's 18 types into 11 card types.
sources: our own comparison of hand-written lists against the field
facts.falsifier: a card whose printed type matches the game type in every case we checked
facts.note: THIS IS WHY EVERY HAND-WRITTEN TYPE LIST WAS WRONG. I built them from game knowledge, which is what a Pokemon fan knows, and the cards do not use it. Each list missed up to 141 Pokemon and contained up to 12 that do not belong. Any theme that can be a QUERY against a real field must be one — a list is wrong the day a set lands, and it was already wrong on the day I wrote it.

facts.claim: @JohnnyCrambo posted 'Do you think caring about Pokemon value makes someone a fake fan?' and got 37.1K views with 68 replies against 73 likes — a reply-to-like ratio of 93% where a normal post runs nearer 10%. He then replied to himself: 'Not my opinion. I want to know what people really think.' His bio names recurring segments (FlashPack Friday, Sun Bleacher) and he runs multi-year physical projects, including sun-bleaching a Moltres card for almost two years.
facts.falsifier: the same question posted without the disclaimer producing an equal reply rate
facts.note: THE MECHANISM: ask a question that DIVIDES the community, then explicitly remove yourself from the answer. 'Not my opinion' makes it safe to reply honestly, because nobody is disagreeing with the host. Reply-to-like ratio is the metric that measures conversation, and views do not — 37K views with 68 replies is a room talking, not an audience watching.

facts.claim: @shotguncaio writes long-form lore and artist posts — an Atsuko Nishida appreciation at 15.7K views, a Miki Kudo one at 15.4K, a Victini lore post at 18.7K — and replies to EVERY one with the exact card list: 'Cards above: Victini EX Full Art (131/135 – Plasma Storm), Victini BW32 Promo…'. Those self-replies draw 1.7K-2K views of their own. He also runs a numbered daily series, 'Day 23 of posting one Pokemon card I love that costs under $10'. His largest post is a single line about a current release at 1.6M views, 120 replies and 15K likes.
facts.falsifier: the same posts performing equally without the card-list reply
facts.note: THREE TRANSFERABLE MOVES. First, the self-reply card list answers 'what cards are those?' before anyone asks, and it is the single most automatable thing here — our editor already knows exactly which cards are in the image. Second, LONG-FORM WORKS: paragraphs about an artist pull 15K+, which is the opposite of the short-hook assumption, and we now hold artist and lore data for exactly this. Third, a numbered daily series gives people a reason to come back, which is what our streak feature is for.

facts.claim: An Illustration Rare trading far above the median IR of its own set is one where the artwork carries the value, because an IR of a Pokemon nobody battles with has no competitive value and no chase status. Measured across our catalogue: Magikarp at 18.1x its set median, Squirtle 14.2x, Bulbasaur 12.4x, Eevee 12.1x, Misty's Psyduck 8.5x, Chansey 7.0x.
sources: our own price data across 15,727 priced cards
r/PokemonTCG discussion naming Poliwhirl, Dragonair and Psyduck IRs from 151 as the set's best art
facts.falsifier: these cards trading at set-median prices, or the premium tracking competitive playability instead of art
facts.note: TYLER WAS RIGHT THAT A STRUCTURAL PROXY IS NOT ENOUGH. An unevolved Basic at 60 HP is the SHAPE of a small creature and says nothing about whether anybody finds the card lovely. But scraping sentiment gives a vibe, and this gives a number: THE MARKET ALREADY VOTES. Cute now requires BOTH signals, because structure alone rates every unwanted 60 HP Basic as cute and premium alone rates Groudon as cute — neither works by itself.

facts.claim: @SerebiiNet has over 1 million followers running the opposite model to the creator accounts we studied: every post opens with a fixed prefix (Serebii Update:), carries a concise factual summary, actionable details, 1-4 official images and a deep link back to the site. Neutral and dry throughout — no opinions, no hype, no questions, no polls, no engagement bait. Multiple posts a day when news is active. Its reputation rests on speed, accuracy and completeness rather than personality. Its own documented weakness: replies and quotes are modest compared with likes and views, and engagement is informational rather than conversational.
facts.falsifier: Serebii posting opinion or engagement-bait content, or a new account reaching similar reach on the format alone without an established archive behind it
facts.note: THE TRAP: this is the OPPOSITE of everything our own evidence says works for Tyler. His posts hit because of his voice, his mood and questions people answer. Serebii works because it has NO voice. And the reach is not the format — it is a decade of being the place people check, plus a database the posts link into. COPYING THE FORMAT WITHOUT THE ARCHIVE PRODUCES A BOT NOBODY FOLLOWS. The real reading: these are two different ACCOUNTS, not two options for one. A person cannot be an institution from the same handle. But Catch'em as a brand could run this model on a beat Serebii does not cover — it reports news and does not report the sealed MARKET, which our bot tracks daily across 207 products.

facts.claim: @Elite_4_J posted 'more pokémon fusion' — three words plus an image — and took 402,100 views, 998 reposts, 13,000 likes and 72 replies. Reposts beat replies 14 to 1, the inverse of @JohnnyCrambo, who took 68 replies against 73 likes on a divisive question. Bio promises recurring formats (Daily Pokémon Trivia, Quizzes & Game Mechanics), claims a deliberately obscure specialty (Mawile expert), and frames the account as a service (Helping trainers).
facts.falsifier: text-heavy posts from the same account matching that repost rate, which would mean the image was not the engine
facts.note: THREE ENGINES, NOT A RANKING. Crambo wants you to ARGUE, shotgun wants you to READ, Elite_4_J wants you to SEND IT TO SOMEONE. And the third is THE ONE A MACHINE CAN RUN: three words carry no voice, so the image does all the work — which is exactly the half we have already automated. A share-driven post needs a picture worth forwarding and a caption that gets out of the way, and that is a generator problem rather than a writing problem. Also cheap and worth copying: a named obscure specialty. 'Mawile expert' costs nothing and makes an account memorable.

facts.claim: @shotguncaio has ~43-44k followers and runs numbered daily series as his signature format: 'Day 90 of posting one Pokémon card I love that costs under $10' and 'Day X of opening one Pitch Black pack every day until I pull the Mega Darkrai ex SIR'. Mix is roughly 40-50% series/openings/value, 20% gm/gn, 15-20% motivational. Value posts cite real market data ('$48.38 for all 11 Illustration Rares' from TCGplayer). Almost every original post carries a photo or short video. Simple 'gm' posts still pull dozens of replies. DOCUMENTED NEGATIVE: motivational posts without a Pokémon hook underperform relative to the collecting content.
facts.falsifier: the series posts underperforming his one-off posts, which would mean the numbering is decoration rather than the hook
facts.note: THE NUMBER IS THE HOOK AND THE CONSTRAINT IS THE CONTENT. 'Under $10' is what turns posting cards into a SERIES — that is our own FILTER IS THE PRODUCT law, confirmed by somebody else's numbers rather than our reasoning. We built the streak mechanism and never generated the sentence. Also: 43-44k is a REACHABLE target, unlike Serebii's 1M built over a decade — this is a person on day 90 of a habit. And the negative finding is the rarest thing in any of these profiles: motivational posts WITHOUT a Pokémon hook underperform, which is a direct instruction not to drift off-topic for engagement.

facts.claim: @tall_alan took roughly 900 replies on one post at ~16k followers: 'What's your favourite Pokémon? Remember to pick something quirky.' The same mechanic appears in @JohnnyCrambo's 'Not my opinion, I want to know what people really think' (68 replies against 73 likes) and @shotguncaio's 'one card I love that costs under $10'. Each adds a second sentence that removes a reason not to answer.
facts.falsifier: the same questions without their second sentence producing equal reply counts
facts.note: THE PATTERN UNDER ALL OF THEM: a question is not finished until it has said why answering is SAFE. Without 'pick something quirky', people think theirs is boring and someone already said Charizard, and they scroll past. Without 'not my opinion', answering means contradicting the host. Without 'under $10', liking a cheap card feels like admitting something. Every one removes a reason NOT to reply, and that is buildable — it is now a register in the line engine.

facts.claim: The Pokémon TCG accounts worth studying are mostly small. @knoyhead ~3k, @xzuyyu ~4.9k, @CardGameNomad ~9.5k, @tall_alan ~16k, @JohnnyCrambo ~17.6k, @shotguncaio ~43k, @Touyarokii ~364k. Crambo's 37,100-view post came off 17.6k followers — 2.1x his follower count in reach. A @xzuyyu story post at 4.9k reportedly explodes far past her follower count.
sources: Tyler-supplied cross-account analysis with follower counts, 2026-08-24
facts.falsifier: these accounts turning out to be substantially larger than stated, which would make the ratios ordinary
facts.note: I HAD BEEN READING THESE AS BIG ACCOUNTS DOING BIG-ACCOUNT THINGS. They are not big. The metric is reach RELATIVE to size. CORRECTED 2026-08-25: this note cited an 18,800-view post and asserted it was already in this company without ever dividing, and 18,800 was an unsettled 15.33h reading. @LongedEth has 21,554 followers (X API, 2026-08-25). 18,800 was 0.87x his count - BELOW Crambo's 2.11x, the opposite of the claim. The settled 127,200 is 5.90x, or 2.8x Crambo. The claim now holds on the settled number, and did not hold on the one originally cited. Retained as being in this company. It also means the ceiling is not follower count — it is whether a post gives people a reason to react.

facts.claim: Counted across our English catalogue of 16,468 cards: Charizard has 62, Pikachu 118, 52 Pokemon have exactly one card, 1,244 distinct Pokemon and forms carry a national dex number, and 377 individual people have illustrated a card with Ken Sugimori the most prolific at 938. Studios excluded — 5ban Graphics alone holds 1,386 credits.
facts.falsifier: a recount giving materially different figures, or the catalogue turning out to have significant gaps in the English sets
facts.note: THE POSTS ONLY WE CAN MAKE. Every other account posts what they OWN or what they THINK; nobody posts what the catalogue KNOWS, because nobody else has counted it. And it is a PERMISSION question by construction — stating a counted fact and asking for the verdict leaves nothing to correct and everything to argue with. THREE THINGS NEARLY WENT OUT WRONG: the prefix bug put Team and Galarian at the top; a name-based count called Cool, Gambler and Digger Pokemon when they are Trainers, fixed by requiring a dex number; and 5ban Graphics is a STUDIO, which would have ended a post asking how many ARTISTS you could name. Scope wording also corrected — English-only, and forms counted separately.

facts.claim: Every Pokemon card image tool found in a 2026 search generates FAKE cards: Phot.AI, Kapwing, MakeACard, pokecardmaker.org, PokeCardGenerator, Image2, YouCam and PromptHero all turn a user photo into a Pokemon-styled card, or AI-generate original artwork and stats. None composites REAL cards from a real catalogue with real prices and artist credits.
sources: web search of Pokemon card generator tools, 2026-08-24
facts.falsifier: a tool that lets a collector select real printed cards and produces a post-ready composite with prices and illustrator credits
facts.note: THE WHOLE CATEGORY IS FAKE-CARD MAKERS. Not one is a posting tool for people who own real cards, which is the thing Tyler asked about and the thing we built. Two consequences. First, there is no direct competitor to the editor, and the gap is not a niche within a market — it is a market nobody entered. Second, the AI generators sit on far shakier legal ground: they produce Pokemon-styled IP from prompts, while we display official card images with the illustrator named on every output. Different position entirely, and the safer one.

facts.claim: Vertical video is 1080x1920. TikTok, Reels and Shorts cover roughly the top 12% with the caption row, the bottom 20% with description and sound, and the right 15% with the like/comment/share rail. Inside what remains, one card fills 85% of the usable width and two fill 41% each.
sources: measured against the 1080x1920 standard and published safe-zone guidance, 2026-08-25
facts.falsifier: a platform changing its overlay, or a real recording showing content readable inside a zone we marked as covered
facts.note: THE 2x2 DOES NOT TRANSFER. Four cards at 33% each works on X and is unreadable vertically — one card or two, never four. And the safe zones are the commonest mistake in vertical content, because a layout looks perfect in the editor and is covered in the app. Drawing them is most of the value.

facts.claim: OBSERVED ON ANOTHER ACCOUNT, NOT OUR RESULT. @parkyspokestop: "Is Team Up actually a good set or does it just have the lovebirds?" — roughly 15,000 views and 17 replies, a reply density of about 1.13 per thousand views. Our own best-reaching post, 2026-08-22-arita-blastoise, took 34 replies on 127,200 views: 0.27 per thousand. That is 4.2x on reply density against 8x LESS reach, which is the whole point — the shape converts attention into conversation far better than ours does, at a fraction of the audience.
facts.verifier: Tyler observed; the 4x ratio recomputed from our own outcome log
facts.falsifier: The same question asked about a set with an undisputed reputation producing the same reply density. If 'is Base Set actually good' performs identically, the mechanic is the question form and not the doubt.
facts.note: THE MECHANIC: it doubts a SET, not a person, and it does not answer its own question. Doubting a set is safe to disagree with because nobody's taste is on trial — a reader defending Team Up is defending a set, not themselves, and no one loses. Leaving the question open is what makes replying the natural response rather than liking. State something arguable and then stop.

facts.claim: OBSERVED ON ANOTHER ACCOUNT, NOT OUR RESULT. @Courtyard_io: "e-Reader era art was peak", posted over cropped card art. A short arguable claim about an ERA, which invites a reader to name a different era rather than to agree or disagree with a person.
facts.falsifier: The same claim made about a single card rather than an era producing comparable replies. If 'this Charizard is peak' performs the same, the era framing is doing nothing and brevity is the whole effect.
facts.note: SAME MECHANIC AS SET_DOUBT, different noun. Name something arguable and leave it open. An era claim hands the reader a ready-made reply — their own era — so answering costs no thought, which is the same property as removing the reason not to reply. Note also what it is NOT: it does not rank, it does not explain itself, and it is short enough to disagree with in four words.
